description: Sub-atomic particles, isotopes, electronic configurations, and how the atomic model evolved.
content_html:
The Structure of the Atom

An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. Atoms are extraordinarily small — a typical atomic radius is about \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. Each atom has a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre. The nucleus contains two types of sub-atomic particle: protons (positive charge, relative mass 1) and neutrons (no charge, relative mass 1). Electrons occupy energy levels around the nucleus and have a negative charge. Their relative mass is so small — roughly one part in 1836 that of a proton — that it is treated as negligible.

Key Fact

Relative charges and approximate relative masses: Proton — charge +1, mass 1. Neutron — charge 0, mass 1. Electron — charge −1, mass negligible. The nucleus is much smaller than the atom as a whole; most of the atom is empty space.

Atomic Number and Mass Number

The atomic number (proton number) tells you how many protons are in the nucleus. It defines what element an atom is — all atoms of the same element have the same atomic number. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so there is no overall charge. The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons. From these two values you can work out the number of neutrons:

$$\text{number of neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

For example, a sodium atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23, giving it 12 neutrons, 11 protons and 11 electrons. Standard notation places the mass number at the top left and the atomic number at the bottom left of the symbol: \(^{23}_{11}\text{Na}\).

Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons. For example, carbon-12 (\(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 neutrons while carbon-14 (\(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 8 neutrons. Because isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons, they have identical chemical properties — they react in the same way. Their physical properties (such as density and diffusion rate) differ slightly because of the mass difference. Radioactive isotopes have unstable nuclei that decay, emitting radiation.

Key Fact

Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers). They have identical chemical properties because they have the same number and arrangement of electrons.

The Development of the Atomic Model

Our understanding of the atom developed gradually as new experimental evidence challenged existing ideas. This is a classic example of how science works — models are revised or replaced when they cannot explain new observations.

Early 1800s

Dalton’s Model

John Dalton proposed that atoms were tiny, solid, indivisible spheres. He thought all atoms of the same element were identical and that atoms of different elements had different masses.

Around 1897

Thomson’s Plum Pudding Model

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed a model in which negative electrons were scattered throughout a uniform sphere of positive charge, like plums in a pudding.

Around 1909–1911

Rutherford’s Nuclear Model

Ernest Rutherford, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired positively charged alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold foil. Most passed straight through (confirming the atom is mostly empty space), but some deflected at large angles and a small number bounced directly back. This disproved the plum pudding model and led Rutherford to propose a new model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre with electrons orbiting around it in a mostly empty atom.

Around 1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr refined Rutherford’s model by placing electrons in specific fixed energy levels (shells) at defined distances from the nucleus. This explained why atoms emit light at particular wavelengths.

Around 1932

Chadwick’s Neutron

James Chadwick provided experimental evidence for the existence of the neutron, completing the modern nuclear model with protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

The alpha scattering experiment (sometimes called the Geiger–Marsden experiment) is central to this topic. The key observations were: (1) most alpha particles passed straight through — the atom is mostly empty space; (2) some deflected at large angles — they came close to a concentrated positive charge; (3) a tiny fraction bounced almost straight back — they hit something very small, dense and positive head-on. If the plum pudding model were correct, the positive charge would be spread out and alpha particles would be barely deflected. The large deflections could only be explained by a small, dense, positively charged nucleus. This is a key example of how a scientific model is overturned by experimental evidence that it cannot explain.

Electronic Configuration

Electrons occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The first shell can hold up to 2 electrons; the second and third shells can each hold up to 8 electrons. Electrons fill the lowest available energy level first. You write an atom’s electronic configuration as a sequence of numbers showing how many electrons are in each shell. For example, sodium (11 electrons) is written 2, 8, 1.

Start with the atomic number (which equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom). Fill shell 1 with up to 2 electrons, then shell 2 with up to 8, then shell 3 with up to 8. Examples: oxygen (8 electrons) → 2, 6. Sodium (11 electrons) → 2, 8, 1. Chlorine (17 electrons) → 2, 8, 7. Calcium (20 electrons) → 2, 8, 8, 2. The number of electrons in the outer shell matches the group number for Groups 1 to 7, which explains why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties — they react in the same way because they have the same number of outer electrons.

The electronic configuration of an element determines how it bonds. Group 1 elements (one outer electron) tend to lose that electron and form +1 ions. Group 7 elements (seven outer electrons) tend to gain one electron to form −1 ions. Group 0 elements have complete outer shells, which is why the noble gases are very unreactive. A good working knowledge of electronic configuration lets you predict whether an element will form ionic or covalent bonds and what charges its ions will carry.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the development of the atomic model, always name the scientist and describe the key experimental evidence that led to the change. Simply naming a model without explaining the observation that forced the revision will not earn full marks. The alpha scattering experiment is particularly well tested — be precise about what was observed (most particles through; some deflected; a few bounced back) and what each observation tells us about atomic structure. For ‘explain’ questions on isotopes, make sure you link same chemical properties to same electron configuration, not just “same number of protons.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms consist of a tiny dense nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in energy levels. Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers; they have identical chemical properties because their electron arrangements are the same.
  • The atomic model evolved from Dalton (solid sphere) through Thomson (plum pudding) to Rutherford (nuclear model from alpha scattering) to Bohr (electrons in fixed energy levels) to the modern model including Chadwick’s neutron.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes an isotope?
A) An atom of a different element with the same mass number
B) An atom of the same element with the same number of neutrons
C) An atom of the same element with a different number of neutrons
D) An atom of a different element with the same atomic number
practice_questions.marks: C) An atom of the same element with a different number of neutrons [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the charge and approximate relative mass of a neutron.
practice_questions.marks: Charge: 0 (neutral). Relative mass: 1. Both required for the mark. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the results of the alpha scattering experiment led scientists to develop a new model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of at least two key observations and the conclusion each supports. E.g. most alpha particles passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space) AND some bounced back at large angles (small, dense, positive nucleus exists).
Secure: Two observations stated with correct conclusions.
Developing: One observation with a correct conclusion.
Emerging: Vague reference to the experiment without linking observations to conclusions.

practice_questions.text: Explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Same chemical properties because isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, so they form the same types of bonds. Different physical properties (e.g. density, mass) because they have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers.
Secure: Chemical properties linked to same electrons/electronic configuration; physical differences linked to different mass.
Developing: Identifies same chemical and different physical properties but link to structure is incomplete.
Emerging: States that isotopes differ only in neutron number without explaining the consequences.

practice_questions.text: An atom of phosphorus has atomic number 15 and mass number 31. Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus and write the electronic configuration of a neutral phosphorus atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Neutrons = 31 − 15 = 16 [1]; Electronic configuration 2, 8, 5 [1] with correct method shown [1] and units/notation correct [1].
Secure: Correct number of neutrons and electronic configuration with method shown.
Developing: Correct neutron count OR correct electronic configuration but not both.
Emerging: Substitutes correctly into formula but makes arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: Describe the development of the atomic model from Dalton to Bohr, explaining what experimental evidence caused each major change. Include at least three scientists in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Chronological account covering at least three scientists (e.g. Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford/Geiger-Marsden, Bohr). Each model change is linked to specific experimental evidence. Language is precise and scientific.
Secure: Three scientists named with their models described; experimental evidence given for at least two model changes.
Developing: Two scientists and their models described; limited reference to experimental evidence.
Emerging: One or two scientists named but models and evidence are vague or inaccurate.

flashcard_questions.a: Same number of electrons in the same arrangement, so they bond in the same way.

flashcard_questions.a: The plum pudding model: electrons embedded in a uniform sphere of positive charge.

flashcard_questions.a: The atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with mostly empty space around it.

flashcard_questions.a: Shell 1: 2 electrons. Shell 2: 8 electrons. Shell 3: 8 electrons.

glossary_terms.definition: The smallest part of an element that can exist, made up of a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons.
The central part of an atom, containing protons and neutrons, with a positive overall charge.
Negatively charged sub-atomic particles that occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which defines which element it is.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, giving different mass numbers.
An early model of the atom in which negative electrons are embedded throughout a uniform sphere of positive charge.
The arrangement of electrons in the energy levels of an atom, written as numbers separated by commas.
